I am going to assume you are respectfully asking a question and I will attempt to give you a respectful answer.

Although all the materials are in place at conception, a fetus is not accepted by everyone as human. As an example: At the beginning of an assembly line you have a lot of components and materials and all the machinery to make a car. But if you attempt to tell someone that the frame is a car, most people would disagree. At some point along the line, the construction becomes a car, but where?

By the same reasoning, a fetus is considered (by many) a part of the female body. At what point does it become an individual human? In early development, a fetus has distinguishable characteristics that are absent is a fully formed baby and vice versa. Again, at what point does the fetus become human? To answer these questions people have used cultural systems of belief. In the western tradition this has changed over time. Earliest beliefs tended to be a time after birth, leading to a delay in naming the baby several days after birth and differing with gender. As scientific principles began to emerge in culture, we got answers closer to conception. Aristotle said a child becomes human at "formation," or when it looks human. He said this was 40 days for boys and 80 days for girls. This is probably the basis for St. Thomas Aquinas' belief that the fetus receives a soul at 40/80 days respectively. These opinions have evolved rapidly as medical technology has advanced. What one believes is still somewhat culturally dependent but less so as communication systems have allowed a variety of beliefs to rapidly disseminate.
